note: Dark done properly: near-black base, surfaces a few steps lighter, white and ~60% white text. The hero is one left-aligned sentence and the real product right under it. Monospace micro-labels (FIG 0.1) give a technical, editorial feel without colour.

Two-tone headline: the claim in dark ink, the explanation continuing in a muted accent, in one paragraph. The gradient is the brand and lives in one place; the bento cards below each show a real piece of product UI. Captured in French (the site follows the visitor's IP).

Monochrome restraint: black on #fafafa, Geist, no accent at all. The hero is split into a short two-line claim, a single mark and three plain lines of who it is for. Proof is woven into sections ("Notion powers millions of agent conversations") instead of a testimonials block.

A centred hero that works because it is short: one punchy sentence, one line of support, one download button with install details in small mono below. The product shot is a faithful macOS frame with the launcher open; the red glow is used once, behind it.

A serif display face on a dark developer site: unexpected and memorable, everything else stays plain sans. Logos sit in a calm two-row grid, then the product is shown as what developers actually touch: a tabbed code sample per framework.

The hero sentence states the category and the differentiator, then the product carries the page: a video of the agent, then the full editor canvas. Three short feature columns with tiny icons sit under the screenshot rather than replacing it.

A centred hero with two buttons (secondary first, primary second) and a very real app screenshot in a window frame. Logos sit in a bordered grid. Long sections use a sticky left list of steps (Build pipeline, Convert leads…) with the matching UI on the right.

A photographic hero (a desk in a landscape) instead of an abstract shape, with the email field inside the hero as the first action. Below, a dark band with a left list of features that switches the product panel on the right.

Small UI pieces (a time chip, an avatar) placed inside the headline make the product legible before any screenshot. The hero action is the sign-up itself: Google and Microsoft buttons, with "No credit card required" under them.

The counter-example to minimalism: a whole desktop OS as the website, with windows, icons and illustration. It works because it is consistent and deliberate everywhere. Note the compact sign-up box in the hero with three checkmarked reassurances.

Two-line hero where the second line is in the accent colour ("Build in a weekend / Scale to millions"), copy on the right. Below, a bento grid where each card names one product (Database, Auth, Edge Functions) with a small real visual.
For a UI-component product, the hero shows the component itself (the sign-in box) inside a soft canvas, with tabs to switch use cases. Left-aligned headline, small grey subtitle, compact buttons.

A large serif headline on warm off-white with an olive accent: calm, editorial, unlike most AI tools. The right side shows a note being written and a call window: the product in use. The pill above the headline announces what is new.
A photo-led hero with a short centred promise and one button. Use as a reference for when emotion, not UI, sells the product; the copy stays very short so the image can do the work.
A big centred headline with a UI chip inside it (a green "Ship" toggle), the brand's hand-drawn characters, then the real workspace. Logos follow immediately in one quiet row.
A short punchy headline, the work-email field as the hero action, a single acid-yellow accent for buttons only. A live ticker of numbers at the bottom of the fold turns proof into product data.

Four plans in plain columns with no card boxes: name, price, one line, a checklist. Only the Business button is filled. The billed-yearly toggle sits inside each paid column, right where the price changes.

Three plans in a bordered row with a left-aligned headline above ("Scale your app, control your costs"). Prices are the only big type; each plan lists features with small icons and one action at the bottom.

Plans grouped under two benefits ("Essentials for staying organized" vs "The AI workspace for work that matters") so the reader picks a group first, then a plan. Currency selector and monthly/yearly toggle above.
Each card has its own mini segmented control (Pro / Plus / Max), so three cards cover nine price points without a wall of columns. Struck-through original price next to the annual one.
A volume slider above the plans: the visitor sets their email volume and the plans react, which answers the real question ("what will I pay") before the feature lists.

Classic four-tier cards done cleanly: centred title, small toggle with the saving in accent text, one card highlighted with a "Most popular" tag and a filled button, others outlined, the top tier dark.
Dark cards where each plan leads with what is included free (MRU limits), then the overage price in small grey. Good reference for usage-based pricing that stays readable.
Leads with the free tier as a fact ("97% of companies use PostHog for free") and a row of monthly free allowances per product, before any paid price. Honest, opinionated copy.
Entries with the date in a left gutter and the title and visual on the right; filter tabs (Changelog, Product launches, From the team) and a search above. Each entry has one strong visual.
Version badge and date on the left, a large visual and a readable article on the right; platform tabs (macOS, Windows, iOS) at the top. Release notes read as product writing, not a bullet dump.
Serif title, a thin timeline with dates on the left, each entry a large image card, title and one line. Search and Subscribe sit next to the title.
Docs home organised by job (Payments, Revenue, Developers) as columns of links, a test-mode code sample below. Search with an AI ask button in the top bar.
The reference three-column docs layout: grouped left sidebar, readable centre column (about 680px), "On this page" on the right. Quickstart cards per framework at the end of the intro.
Installation written as numbered steps, each with its terminal snippet beside it, and tabs for each install method. The sidebar uses small uppercase section labels.
Big black-and-white portrait cards with the result as a caption and a monospace overlay title. People, not logos, lead.
A grid of large logo cards, each with one-line result and a "Watch video" or "Read story" link. Industry filter tabs above. Proof by name, not by star ratings.
Text-only article cards: date and category in small type, title as the main element, avatars at the bottom. No images and it still reads well.
Article cards with custom abstract diagrams in a consistent style instead of stock photos; title, two-line excerpt, author and date in small grey.
Email field and a filled Continue first, then a list of providers as outlined buttons of identical width, with more options folded behind a link.
A full yellow canvas, a huge outlined serif wordmark behind the browser window and one black download pill. Colour and type do all the branding; the UI stays neutral.
Small, quiet headline top-left and the product given the whole stage: the editor framed over a soft painted landscape. Very small type everywhere else; the UI is the hero.

Editorial, almost magazine-like: warm off-white, a serif statement in small size at the top and a large organic video instead of product UI. Navigation is tiny and spread across the top. Restraint as brand.
One cinematic image in a large rounded frame with the headline set inside it, bottom-left. Logos in a quiet row underneath.
Split hero (headline left, short paragraph right), then a tabbed carousel of soft gradient orbs for each voice product. The orbs give a tactile, audio feel without stock imagery.
Huge rounded sans headline on a violet field of floating slide thumbnails, with the AI prompt box as the hero action. The product's output becomes the background.
An interactive collage of work made in Figma with a white card in the middle carrying the sentence and one small button. Logo row at the bottom of the fold.
Heavy black headline left, blue primary button, then a row of small cards each showing a result ("$4M+ in pipeline") with a visual.
Centred dark headline where "3D design" sits in an outlined box and the second line is muted grey. One white button, the editor below.
A playable game scene as the hero with HUD-style monospace labels around it and a heavy display headline. Shows what the tool makes instead of describing it.
Friendly 3D-ish characters and objects scattered around a simple black headline. Shows how illustration can make a crypto wallet feel approachable; the text stays plain and short.
The hero lives inside one big rounded card with a muted lavender-grey fill and a centred headline. Soft and contained, like the app itself.
Navigation as line-drawn icons with tiny labels, a dramatic product photo and small technical type. Industrial-design restraint; the photo carries everything.

The product photo is the hero: one name, one line, two small pill links (filled and outlined), then the device. The rest of the page is a stack of full-width tiles, each one product with the same structure.
Plain left-aligned headline, two small buttons (filled blue + outlined) and the full app right under it. "Product of the Day" style badges above the headline do the social proof in one line.
The app icon as the hero, the name, three lines of description, a "Watch Introduction Video" link and an award badge. Apple-native simplicity.
A serif headline on a painted sky collage (clouds, paper textures) with the app sitting in it. Proves a productivity tool can feel warm without losing the product shot.
Huge serif two-line headline ("Remember everything. Organize nothing."), then a line of coloured tag chips naming what you can save. Almost nothing else; confidence through space.
Very sparse: small left-aligned headline, monospace pill buttons, an interactive graph (WebGL) and logos at the bottom. Lots of white, few elements.
Centred dark hero with a blurred product scene behind it, so the headline stays readable while hinting at the UI. Small, precise type and two compact buttons.
Dark hero with faint code text in the background, a centred two-line headline, a green primary button and a row of use-case chips at the bottom.
Left-aligned headline at the bottom of a dark hero lit by vertical green light streaks; logos run along the very bottom. Atmosphere from one abstract visual, not from many.
Deliberately anti-marketing: monospace everywhere, paragraphs of plain text with links, and a hard-bordered grid of customer logos. Credibility through bluntness.
A serif headline on a dusky illustrated sky, two compact buttons and the product canvas below. Warm and calm for an infrastructure product.
Pastel violet illustrated world (balloons, creatures) with a two-line headline whose second line is in italic accent colour. Distinctive, consistent illustration system.
Monospace headline left-aligned, small buttons, and a dot-grid visualisation below. One yellow accent in the nav button.
An italic serif headline in blue ("Your last next editor") on a light grid, three short feature columns, then the editor. Unexpected type choice for a code editor, used with restraint.
A terminal window with animated ASCII art as the only visual, one sentence and two buttons. The product's own medium is the hero.
Heavy condensed italic headline with one word in pink script, a mascot illustration on a pink swirl, the install command in a dark box and a benchmark chart as proof. Loud and coherent.
Saturated violet gradient as the brand, a centred headline, the primary button paired with the install command as a copyable snippet. Logos in two white rows right under the fold.
Small headline top-left, a large billing dashboard framed in grey, and a short feature list beside it. Numbers in the UI do the convincing.
Clean centred hero, then three chips (Affiliate Programs, Conversion Analytics, Short Links) that switch the product screenshot underneath. Good pattern for a product with several modules.
Neo-brutalist: thick black outlines, pink sticker coins, a big plain headline and a search field next to the button. Personality through hard edges and one pink.
The device photographed in nature (moss, leaves, sunlight) with a thin serif headline: the visual says "calm computing" before the copy does. A small video thumbnail in the corner invites a watch.
Commerce done softly: a thin serif headline, a short line, one small blue button and the rings photographed on a flowing cream shape.
Centred bold claim with a small flag icon inside it, framed by stacked orange and yellow pixel blocks and tiny pixel characters. The brand pattern carries the whole page.
The hero is a question and a prompt box, nothing else; templates as cards right below. The product is the page.
The product is drawn in the hero: a workflow graph with nodes and app icons on a dot grid, under a two-line centred headline. Monospace uppercase nav.
Centred headline over tilted product screenshots in a dark gradient, with an AI prompt box in the middle and a "Watch the film" pill. The prompt is the call to action.

Headline set on orange highlight blocks over a pixel-art mountain illustration: playful but controlled, with only black, white and one orange. Shows how a custom illustration style can carry a dev tool.
Dark page with a glowing green 3D wireframe, a centred headline where only "production AI" is green, and a logo row at the bottom of the fold.
Olive background, huge bright-green headline, pixel shapes and stickers flying around: loud on purpose, with a plain logo row to ground it.
Visible layout grid lines, a centred headline, a large orange-red primary button next to a black one, and monospace command snippets below. Technical and confident.
Serif headline left, a logo row right under the buttons, then the email editor itself. A vertical band of orange stripes on the right edge is the only decoration.
A thin serif headline centred between large planet-like spheres, one dark download pill, then the browser window rising from the bottom. Calm and spacious.
Big centred headline with small icons inserted between the words, a one-line subtitle with a concrete number, two small buttons. The product preview starts at the bottom of the fold.
A left headline whose second line is a violet gradient, floating toggle UI on the right and a two-row logo grid.
Small left headline, flowing green line art behind a docs preview on the right. Light and technical.
Uppercase headline where the last word is outlined, code on the right and an orange start button. Technical and loud at once.
Purple gradient hero, centred headline, logo row, then an interactive "watch a workflow recover" demo.
Heavy condensed uppercase headline, retro rainbow stripes and a terminal card with copy-paste prompts on a brown-and-cream palette. Strong, unusual identity for a backend.
Huge green two-line headline and a tab row of products (Redis, QStash, Vector…) that switches the panel below.
Monospace buttons and tags, a centred headline, a green primary button and a customer quote inside the product area.
Centred headline, checkmark benefits under the buttons and a product window rising from a soft rainbow stripe.
Big app icon at the centre of a radiating line pattern, a small left headline and a row of real app icons built with Expo as proof.
A 3D orange logo object on a track, a serif headline and long-form copy in an editorial layout. Personality of an open-source project.
Left headline with a rotating list of what Deno replaces (linter, formatter, test runner…) on the right, one item highlighted in green. The list itself is the argument.
A big dark rounded card holds the headline on the left and a live list of models on the right; the hugging emoji is the brand. Content as hero.
Hot pink-to-orange gradient, a heavy left headline and a code sample next to its generated output. Developer tool with a fashion-poster palette.
Serif headline on warm off-white with a short line and one dark button on the right, then a dense analytics product view. Authority through restraint, fitting for legal.
A tender photo (a sleeping baby) inside a rounded card with the headline bottom-left and a conversation snippet in the corner. Emotion for an AI agent company.

A whimsical 3D machine scene fills the hero (funnels, pipes, blocks) with the headline set bottom-left on green. A memorable illustration that literally depicts the product (data flowing into revenue).
Large centred headline, a small dark button, then the CRM grey-framed with a contact card overlapping it. A monospace announcement pill sits above.
Thin serif headline, small monospace buttons and the open-source CRM table below. Restrained and crafted.
Two-sentence centred headline contrasting AI answers with the product's promise, one dark button, then the whiteboard UI. Quiet and focused.
Plain left headline and the product shown in context: a video call with the AI's notes beside it.
Dark purple with one luminous arc behind a centred headline and the app below. A single light source creates the mood.
Dark hero, app icon, "Product of the Day" badge, a bold one-line promise and one blue download button, then the editor.
Centred headline with the product name and a key word in blue, a trust line ("Trusted by 250,000+ users"), then the app with a real quote beside it.
Short heavy two-line headline, one purple pill, a trust line and a logo row. Nothing else above the fold; motion lives further down.
A sans headline with its second line in italic serif, inline chips in the subtitle, faint grid lines and two rows of logos. Elegant mix kept to two faces.
Heavy centred headline on cream, a yellow button and the spreadsheet with charts below.
One full-bleed generated image (a person jumping) is the hero, with tiny navigation and a logo strip below. The output sells the tool.
A playful example prompt as the headline ("Make a jazz song about watering my plants"), the prompt box below, floating album-art cards and press logos.
Pure black with a small centred two-line headline and one white pill; a prompt box rises from the bottom. Cinematic minimalism.
A rounded card with a sunset gradient holds the centred headline and the whiteboard UI.
Almost no design at all: a definition list in plain text, two small buttons. Works because the voice is precise and the brand is the community; a reference for radical simplicity.
Heavy uppercase headline on lime green, then three coloured feature cards with real UI (a transfer quote). Bold brand system applied consistently.
The hero is one big rounded photo card (phone in hand, apples) with a bold white headline inside it. Everyday life, not finance clichés.
Bold centred headline with a Trustpilot rating above it and a row of photo and product tiles below. Clear and confident banking.
French fintech: left headline with three nouns, the product on a laptop in a real office photo on the right, mint-green accent and customer logos.
French health insurer made friendly: soft 3D characters and a phone around a centred headline, two pill buttons ("Mon devis en 2 min" filled). Proves a regulated product can feel warm.
A newspaper-like grid of hand-made panels and sticker headlines ("HOW TO MAKE MATCHA"). The brand voice is the design.
A warm photo background, a serif headline with its last line in italic, a yellow button and ratings badges. Captured in French.
The mascot cast as the hero, one friendly sentence and two stacked buttons (start, I have an account), with a language selector strip at the bottom of the fold.
The brand's orange sun character and a big promotion tag on a warm gradient; captured during a sale. Read it for how a single character and colour hold the brand.
Loud uppercase headline on brand blurple with illustrated characters around the app window. Two big buttons (download, open in browser). Personality first.
A short centred headline, the email field joined to the sign-up button and a secondary Copilot link; the mascot peeks over a dark band below.
Full-bleed lifestyle video with a thin, large left headline. Shows entrepreneurs, not software.
A large light-grey serif headline with photos placed at the edges like a collage. Calm editorial luxury for a support platform.
Deep burgundy background, large serif headline, a red pill button and the editor below with an AI chat bubble overlapping it. Warm colour instead of the usual black.
Two-line serif headline centred on off-white, black and yellow-accent buttons, logos in a row. Calm and premium for payments.
Commerce as a poster: a giant italic wordmark and percentage on saturated blue with line-drawn product stickers. Captured during a Black Friday campaign, so read it for the poster treatment.
Four plain columns on warm grey with Individual/Teams tabs; only the most popular plan has a filled button.
Prices per seat type (Full, Dev, Collab) inside each plan, with the products each seat unlocks shown as small icons.
Dark cards with a credits dropdown inside each plan; only Pro has a blue button.
Four plans where the recommended one is a dark card; yearly toggles inside the paid columns.
Serif title, one contacts slider spanning the three plans, the price updating in place.
A payout-volume slider across all plans, with each plan's included limit shown under the price.
A 404 that helps: a short apology and four large cards (Homepage, Blog, Documentation, Company), each with a simple line illustration.
"Pay only for what your app uses" in serif with a usage chart, then plans as horizontal rows.
Monospace title and three tidy cards with icon-led feature lists.
Blue serif title, monospace-ish small text and three cards on a faint grid; the middle plan has the filled button.
Huge "Our pricing" title, plans grouped into Site plans and Platform plans, every button the same blue.
Four cards with an executions selector in each and pink buttons; the starter card is dark for contrast.
Heavy serif headline with the second line in red on cream, then the calendar on a green panel.
Small left headline and a video area with tabs for formats (Long form, Short form, Product demos).
Starry dark hero, a centred headline with a strong stance ("AI for building real games, not generating them"), orange button, then the app.
A centred sign-up card floating over the app UI, with SSO chips and logos.
Pink gradient, heavy two-line headline and a handwritten "Try our Demo" note with an arrow.
Centred headline over a canvas of 3D objects in progress: the product's workspace as the background.
Big white headline, one pill button and the music editor with a video of a musician inset.
Uppercase bold headline, monospace subtitle and small black buttons, with the install command below. Stark and confident.
Blue 3D line structure behind a left headline, monospace small text and buttons.
Soft peach gradient, a prompt box with floating suggestion chips, category pills and dark coloured example cards.
The canvas itself frames a serif headline and an email field: diagrams and cursors around the CTA.
Huge heavy white headline with one italic line over a photo, green pill CTA. A campaign page with full brand energy.
A fine architectural line drawing and a few centred paragraphs about the mission. Captured in French.
An about page written as a letter ("Hi there! If you're reading this…") with the brand's line illustrations of people at work.
The about story inside a desktop-OS window, with founders' photo and signatures and a cartoon. Personality all the way through.
A two-line mission headline and a large candid portrait right below: the company is its people and its craft.
"Help us craft high-quality tools" and a wide documentary photo of the team at work; roles further down.
A short headline on faint grid lines, then the job list with Location and Department filters right away.
A huge "We only hire builders" headline and cut-out portraits of employees each with a concrete achievement caption.
Centred headline on a red glow with one button and a company timeline along the bottom.
An oversized art image (a flower in Stripe's gradient) under a short headline. Captured in French.
Serif "Join the team", one button and links to About and Philosophy.
Dark split: a three-item list of what you'll get on the left, the form on the right.
Form on the right, and on the left customer logos each with a concrete result ("80% YoY growth…").
A multi-step form in a white card over the brand gradient, with steps shown as tabs. Captured in French.
Split layout: headline and a customer quote on the left, a compact form on the right.
"Page not found" with six cards to the most likely destinations (Pricing, Careers, Documentation, API Reference, Status, Support). Recovery over apology.
A full illustrated scene (the Octocat in a desert) with a big "404" and a joke, then a search field so the visitor can recover on the spot.
Small text top-left, a red glowing shape at the bottom and the normal footer links. Brand atmosphere kept even on an error page.
Centred logo mark, "404: Not Found", one line, one button home. The smallest useful 404.
Category sidebar, search, and integration cards grouped under a short explanation.
App store with photo category cards, then most popular apps as cards with a Details button.
App icons orbiting the word "Store" on a red glow, a search field below.
Marketplace with large featured cards, filters and a recently added row.
A big search with type filters, a category sidebar and a count of integrations.
Centred headline and a grid of app icons as the hero, before the directory.
Docs home with cards for GraphQL API, Authentication, Agents and SDK, then guides.
Bright green field with a bold illustration and a short headline: the developer platform sold with the same energy as the product.
Quickstart in numbered steps with copyable code and an on-this-page list.
Brand guidelines as a dark page with one download button and short rules on naming and usage.
A glossy 3D logo tile, a serif "Brand kit" title, one download button, then naming and logo rules.
Brand assets inside the Geist docs layout: sidebar, rules in text, each logo shown on a large tile.
Sign-up reduced to the logo, a title and equal-width stacked buttons, Google first and filled; nothing else on the page.
A plain centred card: Google, divider, email, one dark button.
Sign-up as a split screen: "Claim cal.com/you" with SSO buttons on the left, a photo collage and review scores on the right.
A card over a blurred preview of the app, a tip about using your work email, then SSO options as small tiles.
The product photographed large, the name and one promise, and the price with a Buy button in the corner.
A dark close-up of the device with one line of copy in German ("liebe auf den ersten blick"). Desire through restraint.
A calm photo of someone sleeping and a witty line ("This page took relax & unplug a bit too literally"): on-brand humour instead of an error message.
Product gallery on the left, name, price, quantity and a big orange Add to cart on the right, a customer quote under it.
System home as a bento of what's inside: brand assets, components, colours, typefaces.
Ten scales (backgrounds, gray, gray alpha, blue, red, amber, green, teal…) as rows of swatches; right-click to copy raw values.
Type documented as named classes (text-heading-72…) with live examples and usage code.
Button page showing sizes and every type side by side with a show-code toggle.
The home splits into two paths (Product UI and Brand toolkit) as two big cards.
A component page done right: description, tabs (Overview, Guidelines, Accessibility), framework status and links, examples, and an on-this-page list.
A bold two-tone headline with multiplayer cursors flying around: the system's home sells collaboration.
Colour foundations with full scales for every hue shown as columns, plus an anatomy section explaining roles.
Developer-oriented references with cards per surface and a sidebar tree.
A large light headline on a blue illustrated canvas of UI pieces, with two routes (start designing, start developing).
Colour page with tabs (Overview, Guidelines, Tokens, Code) and a right-hand contents list.
Typography documented as tokens and sets, with tabs for style strategies, type sets and code.
Navigation rail on the left, oversized title in a rounded card, one pill button.
Big rounded pastel panels, a pill tab switch and a clear list of what the colour system includes.
The HIG home: sidebar of topics, then sections of coloured icon tiles (Design principles, Designing for macOS…).
Serif headline, code snippet and live example components (forms, notifications) on the right: the product shows itself.
The 12-step scales laid out as a grid with column headers naming each step's role (backgrounds, interactive components, borders, solid colours, text).
A short centred headline and a dense mosaic of real components (charts, forms, cards) as proof.
Blocks gallery: each block in a live preview with tabs to view code and copy the install command.
Plain language, high contrast, a blue header with one start button and a dated what's-new section. The accessibility benchmark.
A glossy 3D shape, "Let the @tasks flow" with an inline highlight, and two cards (Design, Develop).
Overview with a short intro, one call to action and two large visual cards linking to the main sections.
Centred serif headline and an assembled demo of components with labels pointing to each part.
An inspiration carousel of circular images: brand-led rather than doc-led.
Duolingo's design site as a blog of stories with big illustrated cards in brand colours.
Sidebar plus a gradient header card, then Brand and Product split.
Split hero with tilted product screens on the right and avatars plus rating as proof.
Black header with white line art and a dated version, then large tiles.
Headless component library home that is almost all text: a statement, a link to docs and paragraphs of philosophy.
Plain centred headline over a collage of real project screens with a hand-written arrow, then a long first-person letter instead of feature cards: copy carries the sell.
Opinionated, heavy display type with an italic accent word and a wall of real tweets as proof. Personality comes from voice and type, not from layout tricks.
Shows how to announce a rebrand (Coda to Superhuman Docs) at the top without losing the product pitch below.
Centred headline, two buttons, then a large video player as the hero: the product is video, so the hero is a video.
Quiet centred hero, logo row, then a vertical tab list on the left driving one large colour panel on the right.
Huge two-line headline with sign-up right in the hero (Google, Microsoft, email), then an accordion next to a product shot.
Product window in the hero with pill tabs below it to switch use case, then a full-width aubergine band in the brand colour.
A search box and a small mascot are the entire hero; a giant playful dropdown demo shows the feature instead of describing it.
Dark, sober, one purple accent. Short principle statements (Your thoughts are yours) next to the real app with a graph view.
Hardware as a cartoon object on a flat grey and yellow, giant rounded wordmark, playful copy. A whole brand in two colours.
A company home built from app and game icons as a grid of stickers, with one coloured sentence per business line.
Three-line hero with the calendar UI on the right, then a before/after pair (chaotic vs calm) instead of a feature list.
Centred headline with faint floating object cards around it, then a video and a problem section with three plain cards.

Big two-line statement, a dark dashboard shot, then a large paragraph set like body copy in a magazine.

Full-bleed lifestyle photo with a white centred headline and a QR code to get the app on desktop.

Book cover painted in a landscape, an italic serif title marquee, then a monospace table of contents on a pastel gradient.

Serif headline with a gold second line, a prompt box with suggestion chips as the hero, warm sand gradients.

Warm off-white, plain-spoken headline, product tabs, then three stat cards with customer logos.
Centred light headline over a deep blue gradient, the vault UI below, then a grey logo grid.

Photos of objects scattered around a search box, then a big serif-ish list of brand names: curation as the product.

Bold condensed uppercase hero next to a party photo with chat bubbles, then press quotes.
Short left headline with a small sketch, the real dashboard, then two testimonials and a founder letter.
Centred headline with a coloured second half, the live dashboard as hero, then a 4-column checklist of features.
Dark split hero: big left headline, the review UI on the right, then media brand logos.
Art and hands on iPad dominate; product cards in a dark bento each lead with artwork.
Dark page, headline with a script word, a collage of artwork around it and a green marquee band.
Headline left, sentence right, then a large app screenshot on a soft lavender wash.
Centred headline with one bold word, two small buttons, a dark app shot and outlined uppercase labels.
Manifesto page: large serif title on black, then a numbered table of contents. How to present principles as a document.
Four plan cards on dark purple, an add-on card for the AI feature, then a full comparison table.
Four plans with the Pro card outlined in teal, then upgrade paths side by side and a credit table.
Four plans in one row, Most popular tab on Standard, monospace caps for section labels, then logos.
A members slider updates the prices of four plans; a long comparison table with checkmarks follows.
Leads with Free without limits, then optional add-ons and an optional support licence: pricing for a free product.
Two cards only (standard rate vs custom), then a grid of what is included. Pricing as a rate, not as plans.
Plain plan columns on a faint grid, then a separate compute table: workspace plans and usage priced apart.
Each plan has a small doodle; a yellow band explains the fair pricing policy with an illustration.

The canonical SaaS dashboard: collapsible sidebar, four KPI cards each with a delta and one line of context, one large area chart with a range switch, then a data table with tabs. Entirely grey with black accents; the data is the only thing that varies.
One row of six KPIs above one big line chart, then lists in two columns where each row carries a pale bar behind it sized by its value. No cards inside cards: the bars do the charting.
Huge plain numbers with a small delta, an area chart with notes pinned on the dates where something happened, then compact lists with icons and flags. Friendly but dense.
The KPIs sit in one dark band across the top, so the eye reads them as a single statement; below, a soft purple area chart and two lists with pale value bars.
KPI tiles each with a tiny bar sparkline in blue, a line chart, then lists switched by underlined tabs (Refs, URLs, Source, Campaign). One blue does all the work.

Billing-cycle usage as thin progress meters with numbers right-aligned, then a grid of small line charts each with its delta. Shows how to make many numbers calm: thin lines, one indigo, lots of white.
A deals table grouped by region, with tiny inline meters for ratios, avatar stacks for owners and pale status pills. The header row is a KPI strip with coloured mini bars.
Personal greeting, four KPIs with green or red deltas under a hairline, then a recent-orders table with thumbnails. Generous row height, no card borders at all: hairlines and whitespace only.
Activity told as sentences (Excluding merges, 47 authors have pushed 135 commits…) under a two-tone purple and green bar of merged versus open work. Text first, chart second.
Playful illustrated header (mascots), one green All Systems Operational banner, then a two-column grid of components with 90-day uptime bars and a percentage.
Dark, narrow column: a single operational message, region-by-region uptime bars with tooltips on hover, then an incident calendar. Quiet and trustworthy.
Narrow centred column, a blue operational banner and collapsible component groups, each with a 90-day uptime bar. Red and orange ticks are the only colour.
Monospace labels, latency next to each monitor, big green uptime bars per service and a percentage on the right. Feels like an engineering tool, not a marketing page.

A bank home that reads like a calm document: one big balance with a thin line chart, a row of pill actions (Send, Transfer, Deposit, Request) right under the greeting, accounts listed on the right. Almost no colour; money gets the largest type on the page.

Five KPIs in one bordered strip, each with a small green or red delta, then a stacked bar chart in two blues (visitors inside views). Sidebar groups pages by intent: Traffic, Behavior, Growth, Monitoring.
A serif headline over a grid of bar charts, each bar labelled with the vendor's logo under it so the eye finds a model without a legend. Editorial type on top, dense data below.

A row of plain stats, trending tokens as small cards with a sparkline, then a token table with price, deltas in green or red and a 1-day sparkline per row. Pink is kept for the brand and the one call to action.
Navy tiles on a darker navy, one rainbow gradient title, live numbers in monospace and three speedometer gauges. Shows how a data page can have a personality without losing density.

A trading terminal: candlestick chart, order book with depth shading in red and green, order form on the right, positions table below. Every pixel is used, yet one teal and tight 12px type keep it legible.
The price as the headline, one thin green line chart with no axes, range tabs under it, a sticky buy panel on the right. The chart colour says up or down; nothing else is coloured.

One line chart with each line labelled at its end instead of a legend, a time slider underneath, a country picker with values on the right, and the source written under the chart. The reference for honest charts.
One big bar chart of commits with a range brush below it, then a grid of small multiples, one per contributor, all on the same blue. Small multiples beat one chart with forty colours.

A list of workflow runs where a green tick, a red cross or an amber dot carries the status, the title is the commit message and the metadata sits on a second grey line. Filters are plain dropdowns above the list.
A public roadmap as a kanban: one column per stage with a count, cards that are just a title and coloured labels. The labels do the sorting, the cards stay flat.
A leaderboard with a big search field, quick-filter chips with counts, then a wide table where the score columns are shaded by value. Rank, type icon and model name lead each row.
A forecast as a table: one row per day, icons for night, morning, afternoon and evening, high and low in red and blue, rain in blue only when there is rain. A Table or Graph toggle sits above.
The booking widget in three columns: who and what on the left, a month grid with available days filled in grey, the time slots as a list on the right. Nothing else on the page.
The header takes its colour from the album art and fades into near-black, one big green play button, then a plain tracklist. The artwork sets the mood; the chrome stays grey.
A league table with crests, compact numbers and the last five results as small green, grey and red pills. Tabs across the top switch between overview, table, fixtures and stats.
The stock Atlassian Statuspage, done right: a cream background in the brand's colour, one green banner, then one 90-day uptime bar per product with its percentage.
Navy, with one big 90-day uptime bar for the API and its percentage, then two columns: system status with green ticks on the left, active incidents and scheduled maintenance on the right.
Built on incident.io: one pale green banner, then products grouped with a component count, each with a thin 90-day bar and its uptime. Narrow, white and quiet.
Black, one dark green fully-operational banner, then one row per service with a segmented uptime bar. The date range above the list can be stepped back month by month.

The headline carries a footnote [1] that opens onto a real Paul Graham quote: the brand's own canon used as the supporting copy. Alumni are a faint serif wordmark list (no logos) ending on one number ($1.3T), then a drop-cap paragraph and a strip of real photos of founders. Cream here is twenty years of brand, not a trend: it works because every element is real material.

Startup directory done plainly: a left column of facet filters, each option with its count, and a list where each row is logo, name, location, one line, then batch and industry chips. On mobile the whole facet column collapses into one Filter button above the same rows.

The whole homepage is one fold: no display headline, the hero is a body-size paragraph and one black button, then three numbers and a monochrome logo grid. Restraint as the brand: it only works because the product's reputation does the talking.

Graph paper background with connector lines that wire the sections together like a node graph. All-caps headline and mono buttons. Every card is a working piece of product: a real video player with 'try another video', a live transcript, a cost breakdown with line items, a small analytics chart. A tiny robot mascot is the only charm.

One saturated lavender field holds the hero: serif headline, an inline email + 'Get a demo' form, and the product window floating inside the field. Everything after is white and grey. The colour is spent once, at the top.

Hero is a motion-blurred violet light photograph with the headline set bottom-left, like a poster caption. A mono eyebrow above it. The same violet returns once as a large panel framing a prompt box, then the page goes white with tabbed steps (Set up, Intake, Contextualize, Operate).

An engraved, halftone iguana is the mascot and the hero image: one strong illustration in a technical page. Mono labels in [brackets], crosshair marks on the section corners, a two-row logo grid, then a big testimonial that keeps the customer's real voice ('the s**t out of me'). Dark section below uses blueprint wireframes.

A full-bleed motion-blurred forest photograph as a dark hero, and the product works right there: pick an agent and press 'Start call'. Proof is a customer quote with the metric set in bold inside the sentence, not a logo wall.

A yellow highlighter is the whole brand device: the CTA, a highlighted 'Hello' in a later headline, nothing else coloured. Social proof sits above the headline (4.7 stars, 3,400+ reviews) and the platforms list (iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Web) sits under the button. The hero shows the real inbox and a call on a phone.

The homepage is one full-bleed video (a pilot, a city street, a cell tower) and one sentence in white over it. Nothing else above the fold, no button. A serious-institution move: the stakes are shown, not listed.

Orange on white with faint pixel/dot-matrix ornaments and crosshair marks on a visible grid. The hero is a working input with mode tabs (Search, Scrape, Map, Crawl) and the product shot below is the JSON it returns. One orange word in the headline, one orange button.

A plant drawn entirely with text characters is the hero image. The product name switches typeface inside the sans headline (serif 'Sauna') instead of italic or colour. A deep green manifesto block in typewriter mono, then a sentence with inline icon chips ('collaborates', 'eliminates', 'anticipates').

The landing lives inside the docs chrome: left sidebar with live community stats, changelog and blog; right 'On this page' table of contents. Yellow highlighter on the headline, an architecture diagram of boxes, then a real trace view. For a dev tool, it says: everything here is documentation.

The hero is a flow diagram with one concrete example run end to end: 'Buy trail shoes, size 42, under $120' goes through the harness and a stealth browser to 'Ordered'. Product cards carry a price per task and a named customer. 'Everything we sell is benchmarked. In public.' with bar charts as the proof.
The product window floats on a watercolour/marbled painting; everything else is grey and white. The painted backdrop gives warmth to a design tool without illustrations or gradients.

Deep aubergine hero with a lime button and the real inbox with an agent's action log on top. The proof below is one grid that mixes logos, ROI numbers (591%, 90%) and a quote in the same cells, so the logo wall says something.

A blurred, painted sky with a single notification card on it ('We fixed Support ticket reply assistant'): automation shown as one calm result, not a diagram of 30 app icons. Orange only on the button.

Yellow highlighter on the words that matter (Developers, Agents, all-in-one, Secrets Management), stacked real product tables in the hero, faint grid lines and mono section labels. A security tool that feels precise instead of dark and scary.

Three plans on graph paper, each with the same icon-led list and one yellow button; enterprise is a thin strip below, not a fourth column. 'What can you get with $100 credit?' turns usage pricing into concrete outcomes per use case (tabs: company website, UGC, live stream, gen AI).

A dark hero with a sparse starfield where tiny agent windows float like constellations; the headline is a twist on a phrase ("Trust Docker for the agents you don't"). Below, light grey sections with small, precise UI drawings for each pillar.

An ocean freight photograph as the hero field, with an email + 'Request a demo' field in it and the real dashboard (a world map of shipments) rising from the bottom. Below, a shipment document (INVPO10903, in transit, Shanghai) is the illustration: the product's real objects as imagery.

Dark page with one glowing wireframe object beside the headline and a product video below. Customer stories are logo cells, one of them in the customer's own colour (Ramp's lime), which breaks the monochrome wall on purpose.
The homepage is the product: an empty whiteboard canvas with its toolbar and style panel, and nothing else above the fold. The most literal version of "the product is the page".
A product's goodbye written as a letter: centred logo, one-line title, then plain long-form text signed by hand (Josh). The landing becomes a document of the company's voice; no feature grid.
"Your AI. Your rules." in two short sentences. The product window sits on a painted landscape, then a full-bleed photo of a person outdoors: enterprise AI shown with human warmth instead of circuits.

No image, no product: the hero is a manifesto of short sentences in large light-grey type, one after another ("Every customer served. Every product sold. ... That's inference."). Orange mono caps for nav and the one button. Text as the whole visual.

Serif headline that leads with a ranking ("#1-ranked for realtime voice"), then a carousel of green voice orbs with "Talk to Skylar": you hear the product. The ranking is a logo cell with its source, and the customer story is a big photo of a skyscraper with a quote and a metric.

Dark top with a dot-matrix texture, serif headline, then light product cards (a call transcript, an emotion matrix). Below, a grid of real people photos with UI labels overlaid (Tone, Expression): a voice model shown through faces.

A prompt box hero, then the product window framed by bright pink with yellow 3D wireframe grids peeking from behind: playful geometry instead of a gradient, and the window shows a real generated site (a pelican photo) rather than placeholders.

A one-line terminal command above an isometric drawing of green blocks (services, sandboxes) on black: infrastructure drawn as a small city. Mono labels and a dense logo grid keep it engineering-first.

Product photography as the hero (earbuds, headphones exploded in transparent shells) with a small serif-ish line over it; then shop by category on white, then a black section for one flagship product. The brand's dot-matrix type appears only in small labels.

One orange on grey, everything lowercase, a studio photograph with a play button as the hero. The copy talks like a person ("the operating system you don't operate", "that folder you keep putting off"). Brand by voice and one colour.

Sportswear commerce: a warm lifestyle photograph as the hero with one line and two pill buttons, then three photo tiles (shoes, apparel, accessories), then a large-type list of sports. A ticker of promos runs on top.
Commerce landing led by one full-bleed sport photograph and an uppercase partnership line, then a plain product grid with prices. The photography is the brand; the UI around it stays small and grey.
Each product gets one full-width grey studio photograph with a tiny label and one button: "Shipping now", "Pocket in stock now". Almost no UI chrome; the object and the light do the work.

Car brand landing: one cinematic photo with the model name and two outline buttons, then a plain two-column grid of every model on white with price and two links. Ends with huge type links (book a test drive). Captured in Finnish (IP).

The hero is built from the product's own output: product photos (a yellow shirt) cut out and arranged around the headline, and the same yellow returns across the page. The before/after is implied by the collage.
An isometric floor plan of coloured rooms with tiny avatars in them: "multiplayer" shown as a place where people and agents sit together. A large quote next to a real photo of the customer below.

Dark commerce for a hardware wallet: the devices photographed in a fan as the hero, then each signer as a card with a real photo, a one-line role and 'Learn more'. Trust is carried by the object and a few numbers, not by shields and padlocks.
Real event cover art scattered like stickers around a centred headline with one gradient line. Then the product itself: popular events, categories, communities. The user-made covers make the page.
The hero is a strip of the product's own output: video frames of avatars with captions burned in, scrolling sideways. Ratings (G2, Forbes, stars) sit right under it.
"Markdown notes you'll love" with a red hand-drawn underline, a Mac/iPhone/iPad switcher above the product window, then award badges as proof. A calm single-product page for a consumer app.

The hero is a bordered box: pink headline on the left, a line drawing of desktop objects (calendar, files, a smiling screen) on the right, then four bordered cells (private, offline, work and play, a video). Everything sits on one visible grid.

"Privacy is for the people": a political headline, navy and yellow only, the real VPN app beside it, then a full-bleed colourful street photograph and a short film. A security product that refuses the hooded-hacker cliché and speaks as a cause.

The whole page is one full-bleed film photograph of a person wearing the pendant, the wordmark small at the top and one white button ('Meet your friend'). A wearable sold like a fashion campaign, not a gadget.
A sky full of clouds and a few lines of small type: a phone designed to be used as little as possible, sold with almost nothing on the page. The emptiness is the argument.

Saturated food photography (noodles lifted with chopsticks) with a starburst sticker ('Proud + loud Asian flavors'), then pink and yellow pattern fields and retail and press logos. Packaging colour drives the page.

A fitness app sold by a person: a celebrity training photo fills the dark hero, the headline in condensed white caps, one neon-yellow button, app-store awards as round badges, then press logos. Energy through photography and one loud colour.

A media company laid out like a magazine cover: a classical statue collage with a blue paper plane as the lead image, serif headlines with a custom swash letter, essays in columns, and the company's own software products as cards between the articles.

Each typeface gets a full-width poster card with its own world (a mountain photo, line drawings, a blue spirograph) and the font name huge in that face. Specimens below are a grid of big 'Aa'. Type as the image, one image per voice.

A foundry that writes like a friend ('Try it, it's free! <333'): a stacked text nav in the corner with tiny emoji badges, a video of a costumed figure, then a full yellow field with a big all-caps headline and large plain copy.

Dark page where the hero image is an orbit diagram of the software loop (ticket, code, review, deploy, monitor) with mono sublabels; below, each loop gets a small line chart or radar drawing in green.

A hand holds the phone against a mountain landscape: the repairable phone shown outdoors in use rather than floating. Then rounded product cards with real photos of accessories and spare parts. Captured in German.

Half coral field, half candid photo of a couple: a mortgage product made human. The proof is a calculator: loan amount against monthly payment, Haus vs a normal mortgage, with the saving in a big coral circle.

Two outdoor photos frame a centred sign-up card (Google, Apple, email): the page is almost only the door in. On mobile, an orange route trace over a map with time and distance shows the product in one glance.
A warm peach field with faint quotes in the background, the real library (real book covers) in a window, and the word 'highlights' highlighted in yellow: the product's own action used as typography.
A seal-like emblem, one italic serif line ('We're building better ways to use the internet with Dia and Arc.') and a few mono links on warm grey. A company page reduced to a letterhead.
Inline app icons sit inside the headline words; below, a dense mosaic of saved images (fashion, cars, posters) is the hero: the community's taste is the product shot.

No headline at all: full-width image tiles in strong colour blocks (a blurred giant letter on green, a red chair on red, a yellow field, a punk photo), each with a tiny typeface name. A foundry presented as an art gallery.

The headline sits between big curly braces. Each surface (desktop, IDE, CLI, SDK) gets a pastel card with its own install line or download buttons, so the hero answers 'where do I run it?' immediately.

A candid photo of someone wearing the device with a giant white two-line headline over it, then a flat periwinkle field where the device floats alone with its price. Two moves only: a person, then the object.

Maximalist food commerce: deep red, gold fireworks ornaments, condensed caps and the packaging's own colours everywhere. Loud but consistent, because every colour comes from the product. Captured during a Black Friday sale.

Each flavour's can colour becomes a block of the page; the cans stand in a row like a shelf with pill filters (9g fiber, 4g fiber, minis). Playful serif-ish display headlines. Captured during a Black Friday sale.
A dark, intimate photograph with a big plain headline ('See how food affects your health.'), then a glucose curve as the only illustration: the product's real data shape becomes the brand mark.

A prompt box ('How can I help you?') with suggestions, then the community's own work as the page: trending challenges with prize amounts, verified studios and project thumbnails. A marketplace that shows its supply before explaining itself.

The homepage is a stack of full-width colour bands, each one set in a different typeface at huge size (Schenk, Spectator, New Doric, an Arabic face, Action Grotesque) with its style count. Then plain three-column text about custom work, the studio and goods.

Monospace headline on black with yellow as the only colour. Each surface (desktop, VS Code, JetBrains, CLI, cloud, Slack, mobile with a QR code) is a bordered card with its own install action; stats are yellow-outlined cells.

The real objects of the service on a dark field: a blood tube next to a phone showing your results, with the price in the headline. 'How it works' is four photo cards with UI fragments over them, and the proof is the doctors' universities.

A hiking photograph fills the hero with a short headline; below, warm beige panels with phones showing real routes and small hand-drawn flower ornaments. The outdoors, then the map, never the reverse.

'Type with an opinion' next to a tick-mark clock drawing, then each family as a poster tile (a huge pink 5 over mono numbers, red 'a @ a', a jockey in 'WHITESPACE'). The specimens are posters, not tables.

The key word of the headline ('code') sits inside the product's own selection box with handles, as if selected in the editor. The editor itself follows at full fidelity. The product's UI chrome used as typography.
Very quiet: warm grey ground, a small headline with inline model badges, a terminal window as the only image, then research cards with a faceted crystal drawing. A frontier lab that whispers.

'Feed the facts machine' in giant white type with a small retro machine object set inline between the words. Smaller lines mix serif, sans and outline in one sentence ('Build your customer context layer').

A large light-weight headline beside a collage of real research artefacts (an interview video, a participant photo, a study draft, a chart) with lime highlights. Then big tabs: Recruit, Research, Decide.
A casual photo of a hand holding a can in a car, like a friend's phone picture, with a lowercase line ('calm in a can'). Retail logos as proof, then pastel product cards with tiny benefit icons.
A hand reaching up through trees as the hero, the headline in italic serif, and three numbers in the photo (160+ lab tests, whole body, $1 per day). Below, warm cream steps with tiny charts.

A studio homepage with no grid of thumbnails: a red-lit full-bleed photo with the agency name set small at the bottom, one award object (a championship ring, 'seven years running'), then featured work as a list of client names in a huge condensed serif with hairlines between them.

Near-black brown with one centred serif line ('Rewrite your worth.'), award tags in brackets, then a framed film still. Services are 'programs' listed as text rows. A studio that sells a point of view before work.

Design studio as a pure work grid on charcoal: each project shown through its applied identity (tea packaging, a blue logo, a sign), tiny mono project labels and discipline tags above. No headline at all.
A full-bleed aerial photograph of a client's building with the client list overlaid in white, the current one highlighted. Then one large statement paragraph on white. Clients as the headline.

The wordmark sits inside a diagonal line drawing (the building's silhouette); exhibitions are big uppercase grotesk titles in black with the dates in grey right under, next to the artwork. The building and the art carry the brand.

The homepage is an index: every line is huge uppercase type running off the edge ('WHAT'S ON', 'YAYOI KUSAMA ->'), with tiny inline thumbnails and red labels mixed into the lines. A yellow sticker on the wordmark. Navigation as typography.

An exhibition painting next to an olive colour block with the title in spaced uppercase, then the four galleries as building photos and what's on as artwork cards with tiny icon metadata (location, dates, price).
A publication of visual essays shown as a grid of saturated colour cards, each with the essay's own chart or illustration, an issue number and date in mono. The content's visuals are the navigation.

An AI lab whose homepage is an essay: a light spaced-caps wordmark, one 'new' link, then several sections of plain serif prose with italic leads. No product, no image, no button. Seriousness through text.

Full-width photographs of the hardware (aircraft wings above clouds, a jet engine, drones) in a tight mosaic, each tile labelled with the product name. On mobile, a giant condensed all-caps statement. The photography is documentary, not rendered.
A motion-blurred grassy hillside (as seen from a flying drone) under a huge condensed 'LOOK UP', the photo cut by a soft wave edge into cream. The speed of the delivery is in the blur.
A huge black wordmark across the top, then a collage of a client campaign (fuzzy monster characters with feelings), a short serif statement and a grid of work thumbnails with filter pills.
The homepage is a game of Pong ('Tap to Play') with the score at the top and a tiny nav in the corner. The studio's playfulness is something you do, not something you read.

An ad agency that leads with one campaign: the client's line and logo on black ('Always dreamed.' with the swoosh) and the campaign name as the caption. Work tiles follow, then a plain manifesto in large white text.

A full-width people photo with the programme title on it, a plain list of sections with arrows beside a short paragraph, then a running line of text ('Free programs every Thursday night') as a ticker. Calm, information-first museum.

The collection is the hero: a mosaic of objects from the archive (textiles, ceramics, lamps) with condensed caps labels in black boxes, then saturated tiles for programmes and a design-object clock for opening hours.

A tech news site with a sharp identity: a diacritic-heavy wordmark, each story illustrated with a commissioned collage, a latest-stories sidebar with read times, and a big blue newsletter panel with a phone mockup.

Navy page with a blueprint line drawing of a factory floor as the hero image, then a real factory photo with a paragraph in a bordered panel. Mono caps labels; the industrial message drawn like engineering documents.

A dark photo of a patient using a laptop with the device, a plain headline, then 'Meet our pioneers': patient photos with first-person quotes and their condition. Proof through people, in a clinical calm.

A games publisher: full-bleed key art of the featured game with its title in white caps, then a grid of game covers, each one in its own illustrated style, with platform icons. The games' art is the brand.
Split hero: dark panel with the product announcement, lime panel covered in hand-written product names as a pattern. Below, editorial content (tutorials, artist videos) dominates over selling.

A consultancy homepage as a document: a thin red rule on top, a label column on the left (Latest, Updates, Index) and content on the right, a press quote as the subhead, and an index of plain links. Order and restraint as the pitch.

One client's product shot full-bleed (a car on a saturated blue set) with a tiny 'Lead by Design' line, then client logos as floating black badges and a phone lying on a black stage. The work is the headline.
The homepage is a numbered list of every drop, in large green mono caps on black ('THE PERSISTENCE OF CHAOS', 'BULL & MOON', ...). No images, no copy: the catalogue itself is the identity.
Design media: one striking image for the lead article, a bar of the brand's own events and lists on top, purple as the only UI colour and a loose grid of article images below.

An ideas magazine with commissioned collage illustrations (a hand-drawn portrait torn into red grids) on mint and cream, typewriter mono for metadata, and the print issue as a product. Science writing with an art direction.
A huge faded '4' behind the headline on a pale blue gradient (the model number as the image), then model cards with photo-like imagery and a plain news list.
Greyscale documentary photographs of the robot in a home, each full-bleed with a small mono caps line and one button. No colour at all: a humanoid made calm and domestic.

Orange and navy only: a duotone texture (a heat-shield or terrain surface) behind 'Space born, Earth bound', then a bordered grid of tiles mixing duotone photos, a video and short statements with arrow links. Two colours carry a whole space company.

A family running across the lawn of a house as the hero, rating stars and a zip-code field with a lime button right in the photo. The proof is a well-known customer photographed at home with his saving in a quote. Energy sold as a home, not as a grid.
A top-down studio photograph of the new device among cables and other gear on colour blocks, then a dark news grid of people playing the instruments, all with small outline buttons in caps.

One client's work fills the hero (colourful sponges in a bag), then a serif statement where the key words are underlined links (businesses, people, world) and a showreel. The statement doubles as navigation.
A wordmark filling the width in white on black, a drone video reel labelled 'Showreel', then one large statement ending in an underlined link. Three elements, no grid.
Orange header and nav, a lush photo with 'Welcome to the Barbican' in bold white, then 'This week' tabs and event cards with genre tags. The orange is the venue's identity applied to UI chrome only.
The letters S F M O M A are set huge and cropped at the corners of the hero photograph, framing the artwork. Then exhibitions as plain image + title + paragraph rows. The wordmark becomes the frame.

The wordmark runs vertically down the left edge next to the lead story; headlines are set in a tall condensed face over the photo; the river of news uses small colour tags. A news site with a loud identity in a dense layout.
An interiors magazine that puts the new issue's cover on a flat yellow field with the contributor list as the paragraph, then the shop (books, issues) and stories. The print object is the hero.
One motion-blurred photograph of a person turning, a small serif wordmark and a short paragraph with a download link. An AI voice company that shows a feeling, not a waveform.

Soft, knit-covered humanoid robots photographed like fashion on warm beige, with the product name and a small price and order button in the corner. A man holding a robot like a friend introduces careers.
A close photo of engine parts in a factory behind 'IT'S ABOUT TIME' in heavy condensed caps with a small yellow mono subline. Aviation shown as machinery, not as a sky render.

Each game gets a full-width band with its key art, a short paragraph and the store badges, and the band's colour comes from the game (green Hades II, red Hades, blue Pyre). The studio's site is its catalogue.

A cinematic close-up of a lawyer's face in reading light fills the hero, with a small white headline ('Legal work, without limits.') low in the frame. Legal AI sold through a human moment, not a dashboard.

The model's own output as fashion editorial photography (a platinum-haired portrait, a group in ski gear), with heavy italic caps headlines over them and a lime button. Image quality proven by images, not claims.

Under a blue headline, the hero is a small pixel-art platformer ('Press space to start'): trees, stars, a running character. A durable-execution runtime with a toy that makes you smile, then sober diagrams below.

Sky-blue ground with cartoon clouds, chunky black borders and caps headings; the architecture is an isometric stack of dark slabs with labelled cards around it, and product cards come in flat yellow, peach and mint. A database with a playful, consistent world.

Apple's own marketing grammar applied to a pro tool: black page, a big sans headline ('Picture perfect.') under the app icon and a vivid image, then the Creator Studio suite as a row of app icons.

Runners in a golden field with a hand holding the phone over it, the cute mascot on screen; Apple award laurels in a row and press logos. A fitness app that looks kind rather than intense.

Headlines in extruded, heavy green 3D type ('You're free to grow') over a portrait on a seaside photo. A B2B platform that uses loud display type where others use a gradient.
A dark, moody still life as the hero and a strip of real customer websites below it (LIO AGENCY, a botanical shop) as the proof; stats in large white numbers. The product's output sells the product.

A heavy 'Why is running a newsletter so hard?' among loose hand-drawn illustrations, then the page becomes a long letter in plain prose, interrupted by customer quotes on yellow sticky notes. An indie product that talks like its founder.

A saturated blue field with a heavy rounded lowercase headline and two buttons (I'm a brand, I'm a creator), then a wall of creators' food videos with view counts. The content made with the product is the hero.

A strip of collaged photographs (crowds, birds, equations) behind the bracketed [SCRIBD] wordmark and a big search field. Knowledge shown as a collage of subjects.

Close photographs of the fusion magnet's metal surfaces, light thin type, a nav of bordered cells, then a taupe section with numbered photo figures and an engineering line drawing of the tokamak. Industrial science as an atlas.
